documents.title: Library and ITS Guidance for Faculty on Artificial Intelligence
documents.summary: Library and ITS advice for faculty on AI: concerns, syllabus statements, assignment redesign ideas, privacy and the lack of reliable detectors. It sets no stance on student AI use and leaves it to instructors.
documents.stance_why: The page gives faculty advice and no college rule: it recommends a syllabus statement, per-assignment policies and disclosure ("We recommend providing clear guidance on acceptable use of AI in your class"), and describes some assignments to "experiment" with AI and others students "complete without". The decision is left to each instructor, so delegates.

units.why: The passage tells faculty that "Critical evaluation of any AI platform you consider integrating into your teaching or scholarship is key", a recommendation (should) to instructors that comes before course design (before-course). It fits P63 (advice that instructors try tools and learn their implications before setting course policy); P65 is institutional review and approval, which this is not.
units.anchor: Critical evaluation of any AI platform you consider integrating into your teaching or scholarship is
units.policy: Instructors critically evaluate any AI platform they consider integrating into teaching or scholarship.
units.fit_note: Instructor self-evaluation of a platform before integrating it; not an institutional review (P65) and not training. Coder A had marked it UNCOVERED: advice that instructors critically evaluate an AI platform before integrating it into teaching or scholarship.
units.resolution_why: Coder A used UNCOVERED (restrict), coder B used P65 (neutral). The source is a faculty-addressed recommendation to evaluate a tool before adopting it. P65 is institution-level review, so it does not fit; P63 covers advice that instructors learn a tool's implications before setting policy. A recommendation to evaluate is not a restriction, so unit_stance is neutral. Both coders' notes are kept in fit_note.

units.why: States that generative AI tools "hallucinate" and produce "fake citations or untrue statements", a fact about output reliability, so P31 with modality informs. The page is addressed to faculty ("you"), so the actor is the instructor.
units.anchor: will often "hallucinate" and create convincing-looking but fake citations or untrue statements
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A: all, B: instructor). The page is written to faculty readers about tools they might use in teaching, so instructor.

units.why: Names "bias in the training sets", "unfair labor practices" and "environmental impact" as concerns, which is exactly P53. The page is addressed to faculty, so the actor is the instructor.
units.anchor: serious concerns about bias in the training sets the AI models use, unfair labor practices
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A: all, B: instructor). Same faculty-addressed page and passage, so instructor.

units.why: Tells instructors to "consider issues of copyright and fair use" when designing AI assignments; this is P52 (copyright and licensing) aimed at instructors.
units.anchor: consider issues of copyright and fair use when designing an assignment that integrates generative AI

units.why: Says Academic Technology and Libraries are "constantly vetting generative AI tools", an institutional review of tools (P65, which covers review before deployment); informs.
units.anchor: constantly vetting generative AI tools (as well as platforms that integrate AI)

units.why: "Swarthmore has options for tools that we license which can provide more control" points to college-licensed tools used institution-wide, so P92 rather than P17 (not one course).
units.anchor: Swarthmore has options for tools that we license which can provide more control
units.resolution_why: Codes agree; unit_stance differed (A: permit, B: neutral). The sentence only states that licensed tools exist and give more control; it permits nothing, so neutral.

units.why: Offers help so instructors and students can "make an informed decision about when, how, and which tools to experiment with", i.e. faculty support (P63), the best fit among support types.
units.anchor: We can help you and your students make an informed decision about when, how, and

units.why: "We recommend providing clear guidance on acceptable use of AI in your class" asks instructors to state AI expectations on syllabus or course site, P09 (should, since only recommended).
units.anchor: We recommend providing clear guidance on acceptable use of AI in your class

units.why: Suggests "specific policies for individual assignments" in addition to a general statement, so the rule is set per assignment by the instructor (P04).
units.anchor: a general statement on your syllabus and/or course site, as well as specific policies for
units.resolution_why: Modality differed (A: may, B: should) on two different parts of one sentence. Source: "This might include a general statement on your syllabus and/or course site, as well as specific policies for individual assignments." The recommendation itself is coded in the previous unit (should); "might include" only lists optional forms, so may, and A's anchor covers both forms.

units.why: Points to sample statements from Harvard, Penn, Carleton and Maine, including "a maximally restrictive policy (no AI use), a fully-encouraging policy, and a mixed use policy"; this is a set of examples offered to help instructors, so faculty support (P63) rather than a tier scheme the college itself defines.
units.anchor: a maximally restrictive policy (no AI use), a fully-encouraging policy, and a mixed use policy
units.fit_note: Points to external sample policies at three levels (no AI use, fully encouraging, mixed) borrowed from Harvard; Swarthmore does not adopt them as its own tiers, so P05 (name explicit tiers) does not fit. B also noted it points to external sample policies and defines no tiers.
units.resolution_why: Policy type differed (A: P63, B: P05). The source lists examples "from Harvard that include a maximally restrictive policy (no AI use), a fully-encouraging policy, and a mixed use policy" as help for crafting policies. Swarthmore defines no tiers of its own, so P05 does not fit; supporting faculty with example policies fits P63.

units.why: "We also recommend providing guidance on the transparent use of AI tools, such as writing a statement of use" asks instructors to have students disclose with assignments; P24 (disclose with each submission).
units.anchor: providing guidance on the transparent use of AI tools, such as writing a “statement of
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors as advice on what to require; options are a statement of use or a bibliography citation.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A: permit, B: neutral). A recommendation to disclose AI use assumes use is allowed with disclosure, which is how the other disclosure units are coded, so permit.

units.why: "Most disciplinary professional organizations now provide clear citation guidelines and templates, such as the MLA, APA, and Chicago" tells how to cite AI, a factual pointer; P25 (cite tool, prompt, output) is nearest.
units.anchor: Most disciplinary professional organizations now provide clear citation guidelines and templates
units.fit_note: Points to external style guides; does not itself require tool, prompt or date.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: "Most disciplinary professional organizations now provide clear citation guidelines and templates, such as the MLA, APA, and Chicago style guides." A real statement that points to citation guidance; kept.

units.why: "you may want to thoughtfully experiment with the use of AI tools in your assignments, but there may be other assignments that you prefer students complete without" shows the choice is made assignment by assignment by the instructor (P04).
units.anchor: there may be other assignments that you prefer students complete without the aid of these

units.why: Says ITS and Libraries "can assist you in the creation of dynamic new assignments or the redesign of existing activities", a support offer to faculty (P63).
units.anchor: ITS and the Libraries can assist you in the creation of dynamic new assignments or

units.why: Recommends "requiring a personal reflection or connection to current events" to ensure students create their own work; an assignment redesign around AI (P35).
units.anchor: Requiring a personal reflection or connection to current events
units.policy: Instructors can require a personal reflection or connection to current events to help ensure students create their own work.
units.resolution_why: Modality differed (A: may, B: should). The source lists "Ideas for ensuring students are creating their own work: Requiring a personal reflection or connection to current events" as optional general recommendations, so may.

units.why: "Including an oral component or presentation" is listed to ensure students create their own work, i.e. checking understanding through oral explanation (P34).
units.anchor: Including an oral component or presentation
units.policy: Instructors can include an oral component or presentation to help ensure students create their own work.
units.resolution_why: Modality differed (A: may, B: should). An optional idea under "Ideas for ensuring students are creating their own work", so may.

units.why: "Documenting the process with rough drafts and revisions" asks students to keep drafts as process evidence, closest to P26 (drafts), though the page frames it as an assignment design idea.
units.anchor: Documenting the process with rough drafts and revisions to track the progress of a student's
units.policy: Instructors can have students document the process with rough drafts and revisions to track the progress of their work, as a way to ensure students create their own work.
units.fit_note: Framed as an instructor assignment-design idea for tracking progress, not a rule that students submit AI-use logs. / Process documentation proposed as assignment design, not a disclosure of AI use.
units.resolution_why: Modality differed (A: may, B: should). An optional idea ("Documenting the process with rough drafts and revisions"), so may. Both coders' fit notes agree it is assignment design, not disclosure.

units.why: "Have students use generative AI and critique the output" builds AI use into the assignment, which is P79 (require AI use in some coursework).
units.anchor: Have students use generative AI and critique the output
units.policy: Instructors can have students use generative AI and critique the output.
units.resolution_why: Modality differed (A: may, B: should). "Have students use generative AI and critique the output" is listed as an idea, so may.

units.why: "Instead of summarizing a reading, try using social annotation tools such as Perusall" suggests replacing a summary assignment with a tool that resists AI shortcuts: P35. It is an optional "try" suggestion, so may.
units.anchor: Instead of summarizing a reading, try using social annotation tools
units.frag_end: support in using these easy-to-learn tools)
units.resolution_why: Coder A merged the social-annotation and multimodal ideas into one unit; the codebook says never merge two rules, so they are split. Modality differed (A: may, B: should): "try using social annotation tools" is a suggestion, so may.

units.why: "Instead of writing a long-format analysis, try a multimodal project" is another assignment redesign suggestion: P35. It is an optional "try" suggestion, so may.
units.anchor: Instead of writing a long-format analysis, try a multimodal project
units.resolution_why: Second half of the unit coder A merged with the social-annotation idea (A coded both as one unit). Source: "Instead of writing a long-format analysis, try a multimodal project". A separate rule; modality may as a suggestion.

units.why: "you can schedule a conversation with an Academic Technologist and/or a librarian to help you design, implement, and assess these assignments" offers staff help to instructors: P63. It is addressed to faculty ("you can schedule"), so the actor is the instructor.
units.anchor: schedule a conversation with an Academic Technologist and/or a librarian
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: "you can schedule a conversation with an Academic Technologist and/or a librarian to help you design, implement, and assess these assignments." A real offer of support to faculty; B had actor admin, but it is addressed to "you" (faculty), so instructor. Kept.

units.why: Notes that free AI tools "ingest user data for training purposes", a data-privacy fact (P50). After reconciliation the codes are: actor instructor.
units.anchor: Most free AI tools ingest user data for training purposes
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A: all, B: instructor). Faculty-addressed privacy section, so instructor.

units.why: "We do not recommend entering or uploading any intellectual property, including your own scholarship, research data, student work" into free tools; protecting data and IP, so P50, though it addresses instructors rather than students.
units.anchor: We do not recommend entering or uploading any intellectual property
units.fit_note: Also covers instructors uploading student work and their own scholarship, and it is a recommendation, not a ban.

units.why: "uploading copyrighted or licensed content may violate legal agreements" is a copyright and terms-of-use warning (P52). After reconciliation the codes are: actor instructor.
units.anchor: uploading copyrighted or licensed content may violate legal agreements
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A: all, B: instructor). Faculty-addressed privacy section, so instructor.

units.why: "Swarthmore has licensed platforms through which we can mitigate risks and adjust settings" recommends licensed tools as the safer path: P92.
units.anchor: Swarthmore has licensed platforms through which we can mitigate risks
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: "Again, Swarthmore has licensed platforms through which we can mitigate risks and adjust settings." A real statement about licensed platforms in the privacy context, not an exact repeat of the earlier sentence; kept.

units.why: Tells instructors planning "an AI-based assignment" to "discuss your ideas with a Librarian or Academic Technologist", a consultation offer that helps faculty before setting up AI work (P63).
units.anchor: discuss your ideas with a Librarian or Academic Technologist
units.fit_note: Also a consult-before-adopting step that works like informal tool review.

units.why: "We don't believe that there is a tool available that can definitively detect AI use in student work" says detectors are unreliable (P39).
units.anchor: We don't believe that there is a tool available that can definitively detect AI use
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A: instructor, B: admin). The detection paragraph is addressed to faculty and the next sentence discourages instructors from running all student work through a detector, so instructor.

units.why: "We discourage efforts to submit all student work to a system to attempt to determine if AI was used" advises against detection screening, P39 (not relying on detectors).
units.anchor: We discourage efforts to submit all student work to a system

units.why: The TLC "sponsors regular discussions" in an Inquiry Group series for faculty and staff on generative AI, a community of faculty learning (P63).
units.anchor: the TLC sponsors regular discussions on the subject as part of their Inquiry Group series

documents.unit: Library and ITS / Teaching & Learning Commons
documents.title: Library and ITS Guidance For Students On Artificial Intelligence
documents.summary: Student-facing guidance from the Library and ITS: check each professor's policy, do not upload course materials, verify and cite output, protect privacy, consider ethics and environment, and use college-supported tools. Includes prompting tips.
documents.stance_why: The page says "Each professor may have different rules about genAI use in their courses or for specific assignments" and tells students to clarify each professor's policy. It sets no college-wide permission or ban on coursework use, only conditions (no uploading course materials, citation recommended), so delegates.

units.why: Defines generative AI as "tools that use generative models based on deep learning to create predictive text, images, or code" and names examples, setting the scope of the guidance (P61).
units.anchor: tools that use generative models based on deep learning to create predictive text, images, or

units.why: Says AI is also "integrated into other platforms, such as Grammarly, and chat bots in research databases", so the scope covers AI embedded in other tools (P07, nearest).
units.anchor: tools integrated into other platforms, such as Grammarly, and chat bots in research databases
units.fit_note: Concerns AI embedded in writing and research platforms rather than editors, IDEs or agents; no rule is attached.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder A. Source: "Examples of these tools include ChatGPT, Claude, and NotebookLM, but also tools integrated into other platforms, such as Grammarly, and chat bots in research databases." A real scope statement that the guidance covers AI embedded in other platforms; kept as P07 with coder A's fit note. Coder B coded the neighbouring sentence instead.

units.why: "In some cases, it might be difficult to determine if you are using 'artificial intelligence' or not" says the boundary of AI is fuzzy, part of defining scope: P61.
units.anchor: it might be difficult to determine if you are using
units.fit_note: Admits the scope is hard to determine rather than defining it.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: "In some cases, it might be difficult to determine if you are using 'artificial intelligence' or not." A real scope remark following the definition; a different sentence from the one coder A coded, so kept.

units.why: Academic Technology and Libraries "can help you make an informed decision about when, how, and which generative AI tools", pointing students to human help (P72).
units.anchor: can help you make an informed decision about when, how, and which generative AI (genAI)

units.why: "Swarthmore has options for tools that we license which can provide more control" names college-licensed tools (P92, institution-wide).
units.anchor: Swarthmore has options for tools that we license which can provide more control
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A: permit, B: neutral). The sentence says licensed tools exist ("options for tools that we license which can provide more control"); it permits nothing, so neutral.

units.why: The "Warning" says "Do not enter or upload any course materials ... to a genAI tool without permission", a ban on uploading course materials (P49).
units.anchor: Do not enter or upload any course materials
units.policy: Students do not enter or upload any course materials, including syllabi, assignments, articles, book chapters, or any published material, to a genAI tool without permission.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A: restrict, B: prohibit). Source: "Do not enter or upload any course materials ... to a genAI tool without permission ... unless you have specific permission". The ban is lifted with permission, so restrict, not prohibit. The anchor drops "without permission", so a normalized policy is written.

units.why: "Doing so may violate copyright and intellectual property agreements, unless you have specific permission" gives the copyright reason for the upload ban (P52).
units.anchor: Doing so may violate copyright and intellectual property agreements
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder A. Source: "Doing so may violate copyright and intellectual property agreements." A real statement of the reason for the upload rule, coded informs; kept.

units.why: "Each professor may have different rules about genAI use in their courses or for specific assignments" leaves the rule to each instructor (P04). After reconciliation the codes are: phase general.
units.anchor: Each professor may have different rules about genAI use in their courses or for specific
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A: course-start, B: general). The sentence is a fact ("Each professor may have different rules"); the instruction to clarify is coded in the next unit as course-start. A fact is general.

units.why: "Always clarify each professor's genAI policies before using any genAI tools" makes students responsible for learning each course's rules (P78); P10 (ask when unsure) fits less well because it applies even when not unsure.
units.anchor: Always clarify each professor’s genAI policies before using any genAI tools
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A: restrict, B: neutral). "Always clarify each professor's genAI policies before using any genAI tools" is a procedural duty; it neither bans nor permits use, so neutral.

units.why: "Make sure that using genAI tools align with your professor's guidelines as well as the College's academic misconduct policy" ties AI use to existing policies (P77).
units.anchor: align with your professor’s guidelines as well as the College’s academic misconduct policy
units.fit_note: Does not state that AI misuse is misconduct; it only says use must align with the professor's guidelines and the academic misconduct policy.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A: restrict, B: neutral). Source: "Make sure that using genAI tools align with your professor's guidelines as well as the College's academic misconduct policy." This points to existing rules and sets none of its own, so neutral; B's fit note kept.

units.why: "Is this genAI tool appropriate for your learning goals?" asks students to match AI use to learning goals; P83 (align decisions with learning objectives).
units.anchor: Is this genAI tool appropriate for your learning goals?
units.policy: Students consider whether a genAI tool is appropriate for their learning goals.
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder A. Source: "Is this genAI tool appropriate for your learning goals?" A heading question asking students to check a tool against their learning goals (P83); the following sentence about understanding is coded separately as P32. Kept.

units.why: "Consider if genAI tools are enhancing your understanding or simply completing tasks for you" asks students to keep their own understanding central, P32 (students stay primary problem-solver).
units.anchor: enhancing your understanding or simply completing tasks for you

units.why: "if the goal of the assignment is for you to think critically about a text or to develop your writing or coding skills, then using AI to do that work for you would not be appropriate" bars outsourcing work to AI when it defeats the learning goal: P19.
units.anchor: using AI to do that work for you would not be appropriate
units.fit_note: Conditional on the assignment goal (critical thinking, writing or coding skill); also gives the skill-building reason that P41 explains.
units.resolution_why: Policy type differed (A: P41, B: P19). Source: "if the goal of the assignment is for you to think critically about a text or to develop your writing or coding skills, then using AI to do that work for you would not be appropriate." The passage tells students not to have AI do the work, so P19; the skill-building reason is only a part of it (fit note).

units.why: "Using genAI inappropriately can hinder your educational experience" gives the learning reason for limits: P41.
units.anchor: Using genAI inappropriately can hinder your educational experience
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: "Using genAI inappropriately can hinder your educational experience." A real statement of the learning rationale (P41), a different sentence from the one in the previous unit; kept.

units.why: "Output from genAI tools isn't necessarily factually accurate" warns of errors: P31.
units.anchor: Output from genAI tools isn’t necessarily factually accurate
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: "Output from genAI tools isn't necessarily factually accurate". A real statement of the risk behind the verify rule (P31 informs), a different sentence; kept.

units.why: "Output from genAI tools isn't necessarily factually accurate" and students should "verify those sources and the claims" (P31).
units.anchor: it’s important to verify those sources and the claims being made

units.why: "We recommend you always cite the use of a genAI tool just as you would any research source" is a disclosure/citation recommendation (P24).
units.anchor: We recommend you always cite the use of a genAI tool
units.fit_note: Also compares AI to a research source or scientific instrument ("just as you would any research source or scientific instrument"); the comparison is an analogy, not a collaborator rule.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A: permit, B: neutral); anchors differ but cover the same sentence. Citing assumes use is allowed with citation, as in the other disclosure units, so permit. B's fit note about the research-source analogy is kept.

units.why: "Which tool you used, how you used it, and why you used it will matter" names the details a citation should carry (P25).
units.anchor: Which tool you used, how you used it, and why you used it will matter
units.resolution_why: Codes agree; unit_stance differed (A: permit, B: neutral). Telling students that "Which tool you used, how you used it, and why you used it will matter" is a disclosure rule that assumes use is allowed, so permit.

units.why: "We recommend writing a statement of use as part of an assignment and/or citing the integration of AI generated materials as part of a bibliography" gives the two forms disclosure takes: P24.
units.anchor: writing a “statement of use” as part of an assignment and/or citing
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B. Source: "We recommend writing a 'statement of use' as part of an assignment and/or citing the integration of AI generated materials as part of a bibliography." A real recommendation, a different sentence from the "always cite" one; kept.

units.why: "You should cite any text, images, media, or data analysis you have generated with AI tools" sets what must be cited (P24).
units.anchor: You should cite any text, images, media, or data analysis you have generated with AI
units.resolution_why: Codes agree; unit_stance differed (A: permit, B: neutral). Citation assumes allowed use, so permit.

units.why: Asks students to "avoid entering personal, sensitive, or identifiable information" into genAI platforms because public systems "store, analyze, and train on your data"; P50.
units.anchor: Avoid entering personal, sensitive, or identifiable information into genAI platforms
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A: during-work, B: general). Entering information into a platform happens while students use a tool for their work, so during-work.

units.why: "Always read and understand privacy agreements" asks students to check platform privacy terms before sharing information; P50 (protect personal data).
units.anchor: Always read and understand privacy agreements to make informed decisions about the information you share
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A: during-work, B: general). Reading privacy agreements informs what students share while they work with a platform, so during-work.

units.why: Warns that "companies may have policies regarding genAI use during the application and interview process" and says to "confirm what's acceptable"; AI in job applications is outside the teaching types, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Confirm what's acceptable before using genAI tools for resumes, cover letters, and interviewing
units.uncovered_note: Students should check employers' rules before using genAI for job or internship applications (resumes, cover letters, interviews). No existing type covers employer or application rules.
units.resolution_why: Both coders used UNCOVERED; notes merged. Source: "Be aware that companies may have policies regarding genAI use during the application and interview process. Confirm what's acceptable before using genAI tools for resumes, cover letters, and interviewing."

units.why: Refers students to Career Services (email) to "explore genAI tools to assist you with interviewing, resume writing, and job market preparation", a pointer to human help (P72).
units.anchor: to explore genAI tools to assist you with interviewing, resume writing, and job market preparation
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A: permit, B: encourage). Source: "Email career@swarthmore.edu to explore genAI tools to assist you with interviewing, resume writing, and job market preparation." The college invites students to use AI for career preparation, which goes beyond tolerating it, so encourage.

units.why: The passage asks "Who owns, sponsors, or controls this site? Make sure the company is transparent about the terms and conditions", advice to students (should) to check a provider before using it. It is closest to P50 (prefer vetted tools, protect data); it does not name a vetted list, so the fit is partial and noted.
units.anchor: Make sure the company is transparent about the terms and conditions
units.fit_note: Asks students to judge whether a provider is transparent about its terms, not to use a vetted list. Coder A had marked this UNCOVERED: students should check who owns or controls an AI tool and whether its terms are transparent before using it.
units.resolution_why: Policy type differed (A: UNCOVERED, B: P50). The passage is a due-diligence check on a provider's terms before use, which sits nearest to P50 (prefer vetted tools and protect data); phase is general because it applies "before using a genAI for any purpose". Both coders' notes are kept in fit_note.

units.why: Asks whether the tool "was designed for the purpose or goal you are trying to achieve (such as writing code, analyzing data, making images, editing video, etc.)" and links a rubric; guidance on matching tool to task, UNCOVERED. After reconciliation the codes are: phase general.
units.anchor: Was it designed for the purpose or goal you are trying to achieve
units.uncovered_note: Students should choose a genAI tool designed for the specific task they have (code, data, images, video).
units.resolution_why: Both coders used UNCOVERED; phase differed (A: before-course, B: general). before-course means course and policy design, which this is not; it is general guidance on choosing a tool, so general.

units.why: Tells students to "consult with an expert on campus who can provide you with access to our licensed software supported by ITS" and gives contacts; use of licensed tools (P92) with human help. After reconciliation the codes are: phase general.
units.anchor: did you consult with an expert on campus who can provide you with access to
units.fit_note: Also points students to Academic Technology and the Libraries for help (P72). / Also directs students to human experts (P72).
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A: before-course, B: general). Guidance to students on getting access to licensed software is general, not course design, so general. A's and B's fit notes agree that it also points to human experts (P72).

units.why: Asks "Are the ethical implications worth the use of these platforms for your purposes?" and lists bias, labor exploitation and copyright infringement, P53. After reconciliation the codes are: phase general.
units.anchor: Have you weighed the benefits and risks of using genAI platforms?
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A: before-course, B: general). A question on weighing ethics is general guidance, so general.

units.why: The passage asks "Are you offloading critical thinking in a problematic way by using this tool?", a prompt for students to check themselves (should); it is about keeping their own thinking, which is P32.
units.anchor: Are you offloading critical thinking in a problematic way by using this tool?
units.policy: Students consider whether they are offloading critical thinking in a problematic way by using the tool.
units.resolution_why: Modality, phase and topics differed (A: should-not, during-work; B: should, general). The source is a reflective question in the ethics section, so it asks students to consider (should), not to refrain, and it is general guidance, not tied to doing the work.

units.why: The environmental section asks about "water consumption" and strain on "the electric grid", naming environmental costs (P53).
units.anchor: How does AI surge electric demand and increase strain on the electric grid?
units.resolution_why: Codes agree (A anchored the electric-grid question, B the water question in the same environmental-impact list). Kept A's anchor.

units.why: Lists "College Supported GenAI Tools" (Librechat in beta, Google Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Adobe Firefly), the institution-wide approved list (P92). After reconciliation the codes are: actor student.
units.anchor: College Supported GenAI Tools
units.policy: The College supports these genAI tools: Librechat (in beta testing), Google Gemini, Google Gemini Notebook, and Adobe Firefly.
units.resolution_why: Actor and unit_stance differed (A: all, permit; B: student, neutral). The list is on the student guidance page and only names supported tools ("College Supported GenAI Tools"), so student and neutral. B's heading is a better anchor; A's policy wording is kept because the list is not in the anchor.

units.why: Gives prompt tips ("Define your audience... tone... scope... output") "when you do have permission to use genAI tools", practical prompting advice (P93).
units.anchor: providing detailed and specific prompts is key to getting the best possible result
units.resolution_why: Codes agree; unit_stance both permit.

units.why: "Provide references - but only materials that you have permission to share with the model" limits what students feed into AI to permitted materials (P49).
units.anchor: only materials that you have permission to share with the model
units.policy: When prompting, students provide references only if they have permission to share the materials with the model.

units.why: "Always evaluate your results critically, and check your sources" repeats the verify-output rule in the prompting section (P31).
units.anchor: Always evaluate your results critically, and check your sources

documents.title: Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)
documents.summary: ITS college-wide guidelines on AI: benefits and risks, privacy and a ban on sharing non-public data with uncontracted tools, a review and procurement process, accountability for checking output, and a statement that the guidelines will change.
documents.stance_why: The guidelines forbid sharing sensitive information with AI tools lacking a contract but give no rule on coursework use, saying "individual departments are encouraged to discuss and develop their own internal approach". Stance on teaching and learning is left to departments, so delegates.
